issues.legal_issue: The complaint requirement for offences under mining legislation does not bar police action for a distinct theft offence arising from dishonest removal of minerals.
material_facts: The allegations concerned unauthorized extraction, removal, or transport of sand and other minerals, including minerals said to have been removed dishonestly from land or possession belonging to the State.
The alleged conduct was pursued both as a contravention of mining restrictions and as theft under the general penal law.
issues.conclusion: The complaint requirement for prosecuting an offence under the mining legislation does not prevent the police from registering a case, investigating, and reporting an alleged theft of minerals under the general penal law.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4(1) and 4(1A), 21(1) and 21(6), and 22 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, read with Sections 378 and 379 IPC and Sections 2(c), 4, and 149–152 CrPC, do not create a complete bar to police action for an independent IPC offence. The mining offence concerns breach of mining restrictions, while theft requires dishonest removal of movable property from another’s possession without consent; their ingredients are distinct. The Court relied on Institute of Chartered Accountants of India v. Vimal Kumar Surana (2011) 1 SCC 534, State of Bihar v. Murad Ali Khan (1988) 4 SCC 655, State of Bombay v. S.L. Apte, AIR 1961 SC 578, and T.S. Baliah v. ITO, AIR 1969 SC 701, and distinguished Avtar Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1965 SC 666.

predicates.minerals_dishonestly_removed_from_anothe: A person is alleged to have dishonestly taken minerals out of another’s possession without consent.

issues.definition: When a case concerns unauthorized mineral activity and minerals are alleged to have been dishonestly taken from another’s possession without consent, the police may register, investigate, and report the theft.

issues.legal_issue: A court may take cognizance of an offence under mining legislation only on a written complaint by a person authorized to make it, not solely on a police report.
material_facts: The proceedings included allegations of contravention of mining restrictions and police investigations that resulted in charge sheets.
The Court considered whether a Magistrate could take cognizance of the mining offence on a police report without a complaint by an authorized officer.
issues.conclusion: A Magistrate cannot take cognizance of an offence under the mining legislation solely on a police report; a written complaint by an authorized person is required.
issues.legal_principle: Section 22 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, requires a written complaint by a person authorized by the Central or State Government before a court takes cognizance of an offence punishable under that Act or its rules. Section 21(6), which makes an offence under Section 21(1) cognizable, does not remove that separate restriction on cognizance.

issues.definition: When a mining-regulation offence is charged in an unauthorized mineral-extraction case and only a police report is submitted, the Magistrate requires an authorized written complaint to take cognizance of that offence.

issues.legal_issue: A Magistrate may take cognizance of an alleged theft of minerals on a police report without awaiting a complaint concerning the mining offence.
material_facts: The allegations included dishonest removal of sand or other minerals from State possession without consent.
The police could investigate the alleged theft and submit a final report, while the mining offence remained subject to the separate authorized-complaint requirement.
issues.conclusion: A Magistrate having jurisdiction may take cognizance of the alleged IPC theft on the police report without waiting for an authorized complaint concerning the mining offence.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 173 and 190(1)(d) CrPC permit cognizance of the distinct IPC theft offence on a police report. Section 22 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, restricts cognizance of offences under that Act and its rules, not cognizance of a separate IPC offence with different ingredients. The Court relied on the distinction between the ingredients of the mining offence and theft under Sections 378 and 379 IPC.
